newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Gauteng sees casino bids invited April.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Gauteng sees casino bids invited April.

text.p: South Africa's most populous province, Gauteng, said on Monday it expected to invite applications for casino licences in early April and announce successful bidders before the end of the year.

Gauteng is the second South African province to invite gaming licence bids following the passing last year of national legislation legalising gambling in the country for the first time. Analysts see the move spawning a multi-billion rand industry.

"If everything goes well...in early April we will be calling on this sector of our economy to come forward and present their proposals and hopefully by the end of this year we will have finished the process of licensing," Jabu Moleketi, Gauteng's head of finance and economic affairs, told reporters.

According to the National Gambling Act, Gauteng may award six licences -- more than any other province. But Vincent Maleka, chairman of Gauteng's Gambling and Betting Board, said fewer than six might be handed out if they did not meet criteria.
These are still being ironed out, but will include casino development's contribution to the province's infrastructure, tourism and black empowerment as well as the creation of jobs.

Although casino operations were outlawed in South Africa until last year's Act, the apartheid government did allow gaming in nominally independent black homelands which gave birth to entertainment giant Sun International (South Africa) Ltd (Sisa).

Sisa's managing director Peter Bacon has said that Sun City, the group's key operation based in the North West province, could be forced to close if its revenue base is eroded by competition from neighbouring provinces.
Asked if potentially large job losses at Sun City would play a role in Gauteng's bidding evaluation process, Moleketi said:
"One of the possibilities is to protect the market share of Sun International. But this is only one of the possibilities."
He added, however, that it was in the interests of the provincial government to ensure that there was a net employment gain for the whole country.

Maleka said the board had not pinpointed favourable areas for casino developments within the province, but that there were certain places which were "more important from a strategic and economic development" viewpoint.
Once the process of granting casino licences had started the board would begin with the processing of licences for bingo, additional gaming machines and site operators.
The eastern province of Mpumulanga in January named two consortia as preferred bidders for gambling complexes in this popular tourist area. Sisa, although a bidder, failed to qualify as a finalist.
